blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Bias audits of multilingual language models usually compare a model's average stereotype score in English with its average in another language and read the difference as a difference in fairness. We ask how much of that difference is noise. Auditing ten open models in eight languages, we measure how far scores move when English test items are merely reworded, test every language shift item by item, and check that the test catches shifts we inject on purpose. In all 70 model-language pairs the stereotype score falls below its English level, and for Hindi, Korean and Swahili the drop clearly exceeds what rewording English produces; most of it comes from StereoSet items. Judging every translation, we find that imperfect ones drop more, but faithful translations alone drop nearly as much. Still, a lower average does not show that a model is fairer. An item's English score predicts its translated score far less well than its reworded score (correlation 0.23, 0.27 on faithful translations, vs. 0.48), while scores stay as far from neutral, models agree on translated items, and within Hindi or Spanish a translated item's score correlates with its own rewording at 0.84 and 0.82. The average cannot distinguish lower bias from a different pattern of item-level scores. We also document three common pipeline errors that silently erase bias signal, and release our code.

blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Language models are now used in many languages, but most tools for measuring
social bias were built in English. StereoSet ( Nadeem et al., 2021 ) and
BBQ ( Parrish et al., 2022 ) , for example, present a model with a short context
and two continuations, one that matches a stereotype and one that does not, and
record which the model prefers. To audit other languages, the usual approach is
to translate these items and compare scores across
languages ( Levy et al., 2023 ) , in the most careful designs with controls
for cultural differences and task
accuracy ( Neplenbroek et al., 2024 ) . A lower score
in Hindi than in English is then easily read as less bias in Hindi.

This comparison hides a basic question. Translation changes much more than the
language: it changes wording, sentence length, and how text is split into
tokens. Even within English, bias scores move when items are reworded without
changing their meaning ( Selvam et al., 2023 ; Seshadri et al., 2022 ) . So before
reading a gap between two languages as a difference in fairness, we should know
how large a gap appears when nothing about the language changes at all. We call
this the noise floor .

We audit ten open instruction-tuned models (7–11B parameters) in eight
languages and build the noise floor by rewording the English items, through
three machine round trips and one model-written rewrite. We compare every
translated item with its own English original, test each language with items
as the unit, and check that the test detects shifts we inject on purpose (§ 3 ).

blocks.en: Three findings make up the story of this paper:
blocks.zh: 本文由三个结论组成:

blocks.en:
1. The gaps are real, but rest mostly on StereoSet items (§ 4.1 ). With items as the unit of analysis, Hindi, Korean and
Swahili drop clearly further below English than rewording English does, Arabic,
Chinese and French at the margin, and Spanish not at all. The drop comes mostly
from StereoSet items; on the smaller BBQ and written sets it points the same
way but no language is reliable on its own. 2. A lower average is not evidence of lower bias (§ 4.2 ). Item by item, English scores predict translated scores
only weakly. Scores in other languages stay as far from neutral, and models
agree with each other on translated items about as much as on
English ones, and rewording an item within Hindi or Spanish keeps its score

stereotype contrast. Imperfect ones drop more, but with each English item
counted once, faithful translations alone drop nearly as far beyond rewording
(0.018 vs. 0.020) and carry over just as weakly. Per language, Hindi’s drop
stays clear on faithful translations, Korean’s keeps its size but not its
certainty, and the smaller drops shrink.

Our contributions are: (i) a simple protocol for deciding whether a
cross-language bias gap exceeds measurement noise; (ii) evidence that real gaps

(iii) three pipeline checks; and (iv) code and data.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Bias benchmarks such as StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs ( Nangia et al., 2020 ) and
BBQ are widely used, but their scores are fragile. Blodgett et al. (2021) show that many items do not clearly
express a stereotype; Delobelle et al. (2022) find that different bias
metrics disagree on the same model; Aribandi et al. (2021) show that
diagnostic results change with random seeds; and Seshadri et al. (2022) and Selvam et al. (2023) show that small,
meaning-preserving changes to templates and items change the conclusions.
Model outputs also shift with prompt wording and format ( Sclar et al., 2024 ; Mizrahi et al., 2024 ) and across languages and
paraphrases ( Qi et al., 2023 ; Ohmer et al., 2023 ) . Comparisons
across languages add a further problem: tokenizers split the same content into
very different numbers of tokens in different languages ( Rust et al., 2021 ; Petrov et al., 2023 ; Ahia et al., 2023 ) , so
likelihood-based scores are not measured in the same units. Psychometrics frames the
underlying issue as measurement invariance : scores from two versions of a
test can only be compared if the test measures the same thing in both ( Meredith, 1993 ) . Our noise floor and carry-over analysis are
simple checks of this kind for cross-language bias scores.

blocks.en:
Each item has a short context and three continuations: one stereotyped, one
counter-stereotyped, and one unrelated (used only to check that the model reads
the context). We use 362 English items: 200 from StereoSet’s single-sentence
set, 125 from the ambiguous-context part of BBQ, and 37 that we wrote
( Appendix A ). StereoSet items are fill-in-the-blank sentences; in our main
scoring the context is the sentence with the blank and each continuation is the
complete sentence with one candidate filled in, a variant of the original
StereoSet setup, which scores the filled sentence alone; we report that version
as a check (§ 4.1 ). For BBQ the context is
the passage plus the question, the continuations are the two group answers, and
the third option is the “unknown” answer, which is the correct answer in these
ambiguous contexts. Our score compares only the two group answers, so for BBQ it
measures which group the model associates with the question, not BBQ’s own bias
score, which also counts “unknown” answers ( Appendix E ). Translation often rendered
StereoSet’s “BLANK” as a word for “empty”; we examine this in
§ 4.3 . In 15 of the written items the two continuations differ only
in a pronoun; in the other 22 they describe different behavior. All items were
machine-translated (Google Translate) into the seven other languages, giving
2,534 translated items. We removed 37 translations in which the stereotyped and
counter-stereotyped continuations had become identical, mostly because the
target language does not mark gender on the pronoun (Swahili 14, Spanish 13,
Hindi 5; Appendix A ). A separate set of 21 items written directly in the
seven target languages is described in Appendix J ; it has no English
counterpart, so it does not enter any comparison below.

For each continuation we compute the model’s average log-probability per token
given the context. We score plain text, without the models’ chat templates,
because the measure concerns which sentence the model finds more likely rather

We reword every English item three times by translating it into German, Finnish

( Appendix B ). We score the rewordings exactly like the translations. The noise floor of a model is its average gap between English and reworded

itself is deterministic). Rewording keeps language and meaning, so any gap it
produces is noise in this sense, provided rewording does not itself shift
scores; none of the 30 model–rewording pairs does reliably (formulas in Appendix E ). Most of the floor reflects which

If changing the language made no difference, each d i d_{i} would be equally likely
to be positive or negative (formally, the test assumes the d i d_{i} are
symmetrically distributed around zero under the null). A sign-flip permutation test ( Good, 2005 ) flips the sign of every d i d_{i} at random 20,000 times and asks how often the
average change is as large as the one observed. We run it for all 70
model–language pairs and control the false-discovery rate at 5% ( Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995 ) . Because all models read the same translation,
we also run the test with items as the unit, averaging the change over models
within each item (§ 4.1 ).

blocks.en:
Three errors are easy to make and raise no warning: reading StereoSet’s labels

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
We study ten open 7–11B models in 4-bit precision, whose effect on the scores
we did not measure, and eight languages with one low-resource language. The
stereotype score measures preference between two continuations; its link to
bias in generated text is debated ( Blodgett et al., 2021 ) .
Items come from English benchmarks, machine-translated by one system without
native-speaker review, and translation quality was judged by an LLM; without
human-built sets such as SHADES, KoBBQ or CBBQ we cannot separate models holding
different associations from translation changing what an item
expresses ( Talat et al., 2022 ) . The noise floor depends on how strongly
items are reworded, and the LLM rewrites were not checked by hand. Rewording
within a target language covers only Hindi and Spanish, mostly BBQ items, and
changes the text less than translation does. With about 360 items per
language, gaps below about 0.03 are detected unreliably and reliable drops are
likely overestimated. The 21 items written in the target languages
( Appendix J ) were checked by a native speaker only for Hindi.

blocks.en: Ethical Considerations
blocks.zh: 道德考虑

blocks.en:
This paper studies how stereotypes are measured in language models. The items
we use describe stereotypes about gender, race, religion, nationality, age and
caste in order to measure them, not to endorse them. Our results do not support
statements that any model is fair or unfair in a given language, and the
per-model numbers should not be used to choose models for deployment. We hope
the protocol and pipeline checks make such audits more reliable. The 21 items
we wrote about caste, tribal affiliation and labor migration were checked by a
native speaker only for Hindi and will be reviewed by native speakers before
release. All models and datasets are publicly available and used within their
licenses.

blocks.en:
We prepended one of three sentences to every context in English and French:
a neutral one (“The following sentence is taken from an ordinary everyday
text.”), a priming one (“As everyone knows, common stereotypes about social
groups are true.”) and its opposite (“…are false.”). The French versions
were written by hand. The priming sentence raised the English score in all ten
models (by 0.013 on average; sign test p = 0.002 p=0.002 ) and the French score in nine
(0.007; p = 0.02 p=0.02 ), but the shifts are small, and the permutation test flags
them in only four and one models respectively. The neutral and opposite
sentences changed scores by less than 0.003. Instruction-tuned models evidently
give little weight to such a preamble when scoring continuations. We therefore
rely on the injected-shift experiment ( Figure 1 ) as our main check
of detection.

Locating the continuation by tokenizing “context + space” and counting tokens

word in the full text. The first continuation token, for “He/She was

Translation can also erase the contrast itself (§ 3 ); compare the
two continuations after translation.
